lead: Floorplanning, placement and routing turn a gate netlist (a list of gates and their connections) into physical shapes on the die (the silicon rectangle). Floorplanning sets the core, I/O pins, large blocks and power grid. Placement fixes each standard cell. Clock-tree synthesis adds buffers so the clock reaches registers with small skew. Routing draws wires and vias. Signoff checks design rules, layout versus schematic, timing and power. The result is GDSII (the final layout database) sent to the foundry. Every CMOS chip uses this backend flow.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the flow, Unit 2 for layout rules and Unit 3 for delay.

blocks.text: Floorplanning fixes the physical frame before any cell moves. The core is the logic area inside the I/O ring. The floorplan chooses core width W, core height H, aspect ratio H ÷ W, I/O pin positions, hard macro positions and the power grid. A hard macro is a fixed layout block such as an SRAM or PLL. A soft block can change shape. Pins sit on the core edge or die edge, near the signals they serve. The power grid uses wide VDD and VSS straps to limit IR drop, the voltage lost in the resistive supply network.

Utilization measures how much core area is occupied. Very high utilization saves die area but can block routing. Whitespace is not waste: routing wires, clock buffers and decoupling cells (local charge stores) need it. Aspect ratio near 1 gives shorter average wires; a tall thin core may suit a memory-heavy block.
U = A<sub>used</sub> ÷ A<sub>core</sub>,  A<sub>core</sub> = W × H
blocks.where: U is utilization; A<sub>used</sub> is area of blocks plus standard cells (fixed-height gate layouts); A<sub>core</sub> is core area in mm²; W and H are core width and height in mm.

blocks.text: Placement assigns coordinates to every standard cell inside the core rows. Global placement spreads cells to reduce wirelength and congestion while ignoring exact row sites. Detailed placement then legalizes cells onto legal non-overlapping sites. A common wirelength estimate is half-perimeter wirelength: HPWL = Σ<sub>nets</sub> [(max x − min x) + (max y − min y)]. HPWL is the sum over nets of half the bounding-box perimeter; x and y are pin coordinates. Congestion appears when demanded routing tracks exceed available tracks in a region. Timing-driven placement gives extra weight to nets on critical paths (slowest timing paths), using delay estimates from Unit 3.

Clock-tree synthesis (CTS) runs after placement. The clock net drives every register, so it is a large load. CTS inserts buffers or inverters in a tree to balance this load. Skew is the difference in clock arrival time between registers. Insertion delay is the time from clock source to a register. Small skew and short insertion delay are the goals; useful skew can deliberately delay some registers to help timing. CTS must precede routing because clock buffers become real cells that routing must connect.

Routing turns connections into metal wires. Global routing assigns each net to routing regions or tracks and estimates congestion. Detailed routing chooses exact tracks, wire widths, spacing and vias. A via is a metal-to-metal connection between layers; each via adds resistance and capacitance and is a possible failure point. Maze routing searches a grid for a shortest legal path around obstacles. Channel routing orders horizontal and vertical segments inside a channel, often with a left-edge rule. Layout rules from Unit 2 set minimum width, spacing and enclosure.

Crosstalk is unwanted coupling between nearby wires: an aggressor switches and injects a glitch or delay into a victim. Shielding, wider spacing and layer choice reduce it. Signoff checks the finished layout. DRC (design rule check) checks geometry. LVS (layout versus schematic) checks that the layout netlist matches the source netlist. Static timing analysis checks setup and hold, and power/IR-drop checks check supply integrity. The final database is GDSII, sent to the foundry.

figure.caption: The flow runs floorplan → placement → CTS → routing → signoff → GDSII. Notice that signoff is a check before the database goes to the foundry.

spec.aria: Physical design stages in order: floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing, signoff and GDSII output.

examples.question: A core is 3.0 mm × 3.0 mm. Four hard blocks have areas 2.0, 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5 mm². Standard cells occupy 1.8 mm². Find block area, used area, utilization, whitespace, and whether 20% extra area for routing fits.
steps: Extra area at 20% = 0.20 × 6.8 = 1.36 mm². Total = 6.8 + 1.36 = 8.16 mm².
Spare area = 9.0 − 8.16 = 0.84 mm². Since 8.16 ≤ 9.0, the extra area fits.
examples.answer: Block area is 5.0 mm², used area is 6.8 mm², utilization is 75.6%, whitespace is 2.2 mm², and with 20% extra area the total is 8.16 mm², so it fits with 0.84 mm² spare.
examples.check:
core_w = 3.0
core_h = 3.0
blocks = 2.0 + 1.5 + 1.0 + 0.5
std = 1.8
core = core_w * core_h
used = blocks + std
util_pct = round(used / core * 100, 1)
white = round(core - used, 2)
with_extra = round(used * 1.2, 2)
spare = round(core - with_extra, 2)
fits = 1 if with_extra <= core else 0
print(core)
print(blocks)
print(used)
print(util_pct)
print(white)
print(with_extra)
print(spare)
print(fits)

traps: High utilization is not automatically good: above a point it causes routing congestion, detours and timing loss.
Placement is not routing: short placement wirelength can still route badly, and legal placement does not prove timing.
Global routing is not detailed routing: global assigns regions and estimates congestion; detailed picks exact tracks and vias.
DRC clean is not signoff clean: DRC checks geometry only; LVS, timing, power and IR drop are separate checks.
Clock skew is not always driven to zero: useful skew can improve timing, and insertion delay matters too.

quiz.a: It sets core size, aspect ratio, I/O pin positions, hard macro positions and power grid before placement.

quiz.q: Why leave whitespace in a floorplan?
quiz.a: For routing tracks, clock buffers, decoupling cells and to reduce congestion; a fully packed core can block wires.

quiz.q: A core is 4.0 mm × 4.0 mm and used area is 10.5 mm². Find utilization and whitespace.
Three pins of a net are at (1,2), (5,2), (3,6). Find its HPWL in grid units.
quiz.a: x span = 5 − 1 = 4; y span = 6 − 2 = 4; HPWL = 4 + 4 = 8 units.

quiz.q: Explain why very high utilization can worsen timing even if area is saved.
quiz.a: Routing must detour, wires lengthen, vias and crosstalk increase, and fewer sites remain for buffers; delay and congestion rise.

quiz.q: A layout is DRC clean. Name two signoff checks still needed and say what each proves.
quiz.a: LVS proves layout connectivity matches the schematic; static timing analysis proves setup/hold; power/IR-drop checks prove supply integrity. Any two.

quiz.q: State the difference between global and detailed routing.
quiz.a: Global routing assigns nets to regions or tracks and estimates congestion; detailed routing chooses exact tracks, widths, spacing and vias.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, physical design teams use commercial place-and-route tools and run many signoff corners. At advanced nodes, double patterning, coloring and electromigration checks become part of routing. Research explores machine-learning placement, 3D stacked dies and chiplet routing. Search for physical design flow, clock-tree synthesis, global routing congestion and IR-drop signoff to go deeper.
